stem: If both book shops got 10 % profit in the month of August 2017, find the profit for each book seller in each subject in that month.
If \(A = \begin{bmatrix} a_{11} & a_{12} & a_{13} \end{bmatrix}\) and \(B = \begin{bmatrix} b_{11} \\ b_{21} \\ b_{31} \end{bmatrix}\), find \(AB\).
solution:
Since number of columns of \(A\) = number of rows of \(B\) = 3

Therefore product \(AB\) is defined and its order is 1.

\((A)_{1\times 3}\,(B)_{3\times 1} = (AB)_{1\times 1}\)

\(AB = \begin{bmatrix} a_{11}\times b_{11} + a_{12}\times b_{21} + a_{13}\times b_{31} \end{bmatrix}\)

stem: Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}_{1\times 3}\) and \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}_{3\times 1}\), find \(AB\). Does \(BA\) exist? If yes, find it.
solution:
Product \(AB\) is defined and order of \(AB\) is 1.

\(\therefore AB = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1\times 3 + 3\times 2 + 2\times 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 11 \end{bmatrix}_{1\times 1}\)

Again since number of column of \(B\) = number of rows of \(A = 1\)

\(\therefore\) The product \(BA\) also is defined and order of \(BA\) is 3.

\(BA = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}_{3\times 1}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}_{1\times 3} = \begin{bmatrix} 3\times 1 & 3\times 3 & 3\times 2 \\ 2\times 1 & 2\times 3 & 2\times 2 \\ 1\times 1 & 1\times 3 & 1\times 2 \end{bmatrix}_{3\times 3} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 9 & 6 \\ 2 & 6 & 4 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}_{3\times 3}\)

Remark : Here \(AB\) and \(BA\) both are defined but \(AB \ne BA\).

stem: \(A = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & -2 \\ -3 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}_{3\times 2}\), \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2 \end{bmatrix}_{2\times 2}\). Find \(AB\) and \(BA\) which ever exist.
solution:
Here \(A\) is order of \(3 \times 2\) and \(B\) is of order \(2 \times 2\). By conformability of product, \(AB\) is defined but \(BA\) is not defined.

\(\therefore AB = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & -2 \\ -3 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ -1 & -2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1+2 & -2+4 \\ -3-2 & -6-4 \\ 1+0 & 2+0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ -5 & -10 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\)

stem: Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 & -1 \\ -2 & 5 & 4 \end{bmatrix}_{2\times 3}\), \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -3 \\ -4 & 2 \end{bmatrix}_{2\times 2}\). Find \(AB\) and \(BA\) which ever exist.
solution:
Since number of columns of \(A \ne\) number of rows of \(B\). Product of \(AB\) is not defined. But number of columns of \(B\) = number of rows of \(A = 2\), the product \(BA\) exists,

\(\therefore BA = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -3 \\ -4 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 & -1 \\ -2 & 5 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\)

\(= \begin{bmatrix} 9+6 & 6-15 & -3-12 \\ -12-4 & -8+10 & 4+8 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 15 & -9 & -15 \\ -16 & 2 & 12 \end{bmatrix}\)

stem: Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -3 \\ 5 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(B = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 3 \\ 4 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\). Find \(AB\) and \(BA\) which ever exist.
solution:
Since \(A\) and \(B\) are two matrix of same order \(2 \times 2\).

\(\therefore\) Both the product \(AB\) and \(BA\) exist and are of same order \(2 \times 2\)

\(AB = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -3 \\ 5 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} -1 & 3 \\ 4 & -2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -4-12 & 12+6 \\ -5+8 & 15-4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -16 & 18 \\ 3 & 11 \end{bmatrix}\)

\(BA = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 3 \\ 4 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 4 & -3 \\ 5 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -4+15 & 3+6 \\ 16-10 & -12-4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 11 & 9 \\ 6 & -16 \end{bmatrix}\)

Here \(AB \ne BA\)

If \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 & 3 \\ 3 & 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) prove that \(A^2 - 5A\) is a scalar matrix.
solution:
Let \(A^2 = A.A\)

\(= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 & 3 \\ 3 & 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 & 3 \\ 3 & 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\)

\(= \begin{bmatrix} 1+9+9 & 3+3+9 & 3+9+3 \\ 3+3+9 & 9+1+9 & 9+3+3 \\ 3+9+3 & 9+3+3 & 9+9+1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 19 & 15 & 15 \\ 15 & 19 & 15 \\ 15 & 15 & 19 \end{bmatrix}\)

\(\therefore A^2 - 5A = \begin{bmatrix} 19 & 15 & 15 \\ 15 & 19 & 15 \\ 15 & 15 & 19 \end{bmatrix} - 5\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 & 3 \\ 3 & 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\)

\(= \begin{bmatrix} 19 & 15 & 15 \\ 15 & 19 & 15 \\ 15 & 15 & 19 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 15 & 15 \\ 15 & 5 & 15 \\ 15 & 15 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\)

\(\therefore A^2 - 5A = \begin{bmatrix} 14 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 14 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 14 \end{bmatrix} = 14I\)

\(\therefore A^2 - 5A\) is a scalar matrix.

stem: If \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ 4 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\), find \(k\), so that \(A^2 - kA + 2I = O\), where \(I\) is an identity matrix and \(O\) is null matrix of order 2.
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the printed solution shows \(-2 + k = 0\) beside \(\therefore 2k = 2\); the matrix entry is \(-2 + 2k\). The final answer is unaffected.]

Given \(A^2 - kA + 2I = O\)

\(\therefore\) Here, \(A^2 = AA = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ 4 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ 4 & -2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 9-8 & -6+4 \\ 12-8 & -8+4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ 4 & -4 \end{bmatrix}\)

\(\therefore A^2 - kA + 2I = O\)

\(\therefore \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ 4 & -4 \end{bmatrix} - k\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ 4 & -2 \end{bmatrix} + 2\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = O\)

\(\therefore \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2 \\ 4 & -4 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 3k & -2k \\ 4k & -2k \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\)

\(\therefore \begin{bmatrix} 1 - 3k + 2 & -2 + 2k \\ 4 - 4k & -4 + 2k + 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\)

\(\therefore\) Using definition of equality of matrices, we have

\(1 - 3k + 2 = 0 \quad \therefore 3k = 3\)

\(-2 + k = 0 \quad \therefore 2k = 2\)

\(4 - 4k = 0 \quad \therefore 4k = 4\)

\(-4 + 2k + 2 = 0 \quad \therefore 2k = 2\)

\(\therefore k = 1\)
_note: Printed defect in the book's own solution: the second equation is printed as "\(-2 + k = 0\)" beside "\(\therefore 2k = 2\)"; from the matrix entry \(-2 + 2k = 0\) the left side should read \(-2 + 2k = 0\).

stem: Find \(x\) and \(y\), if \(\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\left\{ 3\begin{bmatrix} 6 & 3 \\ -1 & 2 \\ 5 & 4 \end{bmatrix} + 2\begin{bmatrix} -4 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ -3 & -4 \end{bmatrix} \right\} = \begin{bmatrix} x & y \end{bmatrix}\)
solution:
Given \(\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\left\{ 3\begin{bmatrix} 6 & 3 \\ -1 & 2 \\ 5 & 4 \end{bmatrix} + 2\begin{bmatrix} -4 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ -3 & -4 \end{bmatrix} \right\} = \begin{bmatrix} x & y \end{bmatrix}\)

\(\therefore \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\left\{ \begin{bmatrix} 18 & 9 \\ -3 & 6 \\ 15 & 12 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} -8 & -2 \\ 2 & 0 \\ -6 & -8 \end{bmatrix} \right\} = \begin{bmatrix} x & y \end{bmatrix}\)

\(\therefore \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 10 & 7 \\ -1 & 6 \\ 9 & 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} x & y \end{bmatrix}\)

\(\therefore \begin{bmatrix} 20 + 27 & 14 + 12 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} x & y \end{bmatrix}\)

\(\therefore \begin{bmatrix} 47 & 26 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} x & y \end{bmatrix} \quad \therefore x = 47,\ y = 26\) by definition of equality of matrices.

stem: Find if \(\begin{bmatrix} \sin\theta \\ \cos\theta \\ \theta \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} \sin\theta & \cos\theta & \theta \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 17 \end{bmatrix}\)
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the stem reads 'Find if' with the \(\theta\) missing, and the product is printed as column \(\times\) row (which would be \(3 \times 3\)) while the solution computes row \(\times\) column. The printed spelling 'matries' is kept as it appears.]

Let \(\begin{bmatrix} \sin\theta \\ \cos\theta \\ \theta \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} \sin\theta & \cos\theta & \theta \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 17 \end{bmatrix}\),

\(\therefore \begin{bmatrix} \sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta + \theta^2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 17 \end{bmatrix}\)

\(\therefore\) By definition of equality of matrices

\(\therefore 1 + \theta^2 = 17 \quad \therefore \theta^2 = 17 - 1 \quad \therefore \theta^2 = 16,\)

\(\therefore \theta = \pm 4\)
_note: Two printed defects. (1) The stem reads "Find if" — the quantity to be found (\(\theta\)) is missing. (2) As printed the product is a \(3\times1\) column times a \(1\times3\) row, which is a \(3\times3\) matrix, not \([17]\); the book's own solution computes the row-times-column product \(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta + \theta^2\), so the two factors are printed in the wrong order. The book also prints "matries" for "matrices".

stem: If \(A = \begin{bmatrix} a & 0 \\ 0 & b \end{bmatrix}\), prove that \(A^n = \begin{bmatrix} a^n & 0 \\ 0 & b^n \end{bmatrix}\) for all \(n \in N\).
solution:
Given \(A = \begin{bmatrix} a & 0 \\ 0 & b \end{bmatrix}\)

We prove \(A^n = \begin{bmatrix} a^n & 0 \\ 0 & b^n \end{bmatrix}\) for all \(n \in N\) using mathematical induction

Let \(P(n)\) be \(= \begin{bmatrix} a^n & 0 \\ 0 & b^n \end{bmatrix}\) for \(n \in N\).

To prove that \(P(n)\) is true for \(n = 1\)

\(P(1)\) is \(A^1 = A = \begin{bmatrix} a & 0 \\ 0 & b \end{bmatrix}\) \(\therefore P(1)\) is true.

Assume that \(P(K)\) is true for some \(K \in N\)

That is \(P(K)\) is \(A^k = \begin{bmatrix} a^K & 0 \\ 0 & b^K \end{bmatrix}\)

To prove that \(P(K) \to P(K+1)\) is true consider L.H.S. of \(P(K+1)\)

That is \(A^{k+1} = A^k.A = \begin{bmatrix} a^K & 0 \\ 0 & b^K \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} a & 0 \\ 0 & b \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} a^{K+1}+0 & 0+0 \\ 0+0 & b^{K+1}+0 \end{bmatrix}\)

\(= \begin{bmatrix} a^{K+1} & 0 \\ 0 & b^{K+1} \end{bmatrix} = \) R.H.S of \(P(K+1)\)

Hence \(P(K+1)\) is true.

\(\therefore P(K) \Rightarrow P(K+1)\) for all \(K \in N\)

Hence by principle of mathematical induction, the statement \(P(n)\) is true for all \(n \in N\).

That is \(P(n)\) is true \(\to P(2)\) is true \(\to P(3)\) is true and so on \(\to P(n)\) is true, \(n \in N\).

\(\therefore A^n = \begin{bmatrix} a^n & 0 \\ 0 & b^n \end{bmatrix}\) for all \(n \in N\).

stem: A school purchased 8 dozen Mathematics books, 7 dozen Physics books and 10 dozen Chemistry books, the prices are Rs.50, Rs.40 and Rs.60 per book respectively. Find the total amount that the book seller will receive from school authority using matrix multiplication.
solution:
Let \(A\) be the column matrix of books of different subjects and let \(B\) be the row matrix of prices of one book of each subject.

\(A = \begin{bmatrix} 8\times 12 \\ 7\times 12 \\ 10\times 12 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 96 \\ 84 \\ 120 \end{bmatrix}\), \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 50 & 40 & 60 \end{bmatrix}\)

\(\therefore\) The total amount received by the bookseller is obtained by matrix \(BA\).

\(\therefore BA = \begin{bmatrix} 50 & 40 & 60 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 96 \\ 84 \\ 120 \end{bmatrix}\)

\(= \begin{bmatrix} 50\times 96 + 40\times 84 + 60\times 120 \end{bmatrix}\)

\(= \begin{bmatrix} 4800 + 3360 + 7200 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 15360 \end{bmatrix}\)

Thus the amount received by the bookseller from the school is Rs.15360.

| | Kabaddi | Cricket | Tennis |
|---|---|---|---|
| Modern School | 20 | 35 | 15 |
| Progressive School | 18 | 36 | 12 |
| Sharada Sadan | 24 | 12 | 8 |
| Vidya Niketan | 25 | 20 | 6 |

The charges per student for each game are given below-

| | Coach | E & M |
|---|---|---|
| Kabaddi | 40 | 10 |
| Cricket | 50 | 50 |
| Tennis | 60 | 40 |

E and M is for equipment and maintain.

Find the expense of each school on Coaching and on E and M by multiplication of the above matrices.
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the printed worked solution is defective in several places. Its data table gives Modern School 18 for Tennis where the question's table gives 15; the first row of the expansion pairs \(36 \times 50\) with the value \(1750 = 35 \times 50\); \(18 \times 60 = 1080\) is printed as \(108\); and the final matrix contradicts its own expansion in two cells (2650 against 2658, and 2960 against 2460). The solution above is a corrected derivation from the question's own table. The printed question also states no task — the closing sentence of the stem reproduces the instruction that opens the book's working.]

Let \(S\) be the matrix of students and \(C\) the matrix of charges per student. The expense of each school on Coaching and on E & M is the product \(SC\).

\(SC = \begin{bmatrix} 20 & 35 & 15 \\ 18 & 36 & 12 \\ 24 & 12 & 8 \\ 25 & 20 & 6 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 40 & 10 \\ 50 & 50 \\ 60 & 40 \end{bmatrix}\)

\(= \begin{bmatrix} 800+1750+900 & 200+1750+600 \\ 720+1800+720 & 180+1800+480 \\ 960+600+480 & 240+600+320 \\ 1000+1000+360 & 250+1000+240 \end{bmatrix}\)

\(= \begin{bmatrix} 3450 & 2550 \\ 3240 & 2460 \\ 2040 & 1160 \\ 2360 & 1490 \end{bmatrix}\)

Taking the rows in the order Modern School, Progressive School, Sharada Sadan, Vidya Niketan, the expense on Coaching is \(3450, 3240, 2040, 2360\) and on equipment and maintenance is \(2550, 2460, 1160, 1490\) respectively.
_note: Heavily defective as printed; transcribed faithfully. (1) The stem states no question at all — the task is only implied by the line that opens the working; the final sentence of the stem here paraphrases that line so the question is answerable. (2) Spelling/wording defects preserved: "standidium", "There center charge fee is changed pen student", "as well as 4 equipment and maintenances", "fourd", "matrics", "Progreesive", "Sharda School", "Sharada Sadan" vs "Sharada". (3) The Modern-School Tennis entry is 15 in the question's table but 18 in the working's table and in the products. (4) The Modern-School Coaching product line prints \(36\times50\) although the Cricket entry is 35, yet the numeric line beneath it prints 1750 \((=35\times50)\); and \(18\times60=1080\) is printed as 108. (5) The final matrix disagrees with its own expansion in two cells: row 1 col 1 prints 2650 where \(800+1750+108=2658\), and row 2 col 2 prints 2960 where \(180+1800+480=2460\).
